nameStory: The 'leatherleaf' part of this shrub's name comes from its thick, glossy evergreen leaves that feel remarkably tough and waxy to the touch, much like fine leather. It's also called 'mahonia' after Bernard McMahon, an Irish-American botanist who helped popularize many ornamental plants in early America, though botanists now classify it in the barberry genus.
description: Leatherleaf mahonia is a striking evergreen shrub that grows 6-10 feet tall with an upright, somewhat sparse branching pattern. Its most distinctive features are its large, compound leaves made up of thick, spiny-edged leaflets that look almost artificial in their glossy perfection. This Chinese native was brought to America as an ornamental plant and has occasionally escaped gardens to grow wild, though it remains quite rare in New England with only a handful of documented sightings.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Large compound leaves with 9-15 thick, leathery leaflets arranged in pairs along a central stem. Each leaflet has sharp spines along the edges and feels waxy and substantial, almost like plastic. The leaves stay green year-round and have a distinctive blue-green color.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Upright evergreen shrub reaching 6-10 feet tall with somewhat open, leggy branching. The thick stems are yellowish and the overall plant has a bold, architectural appearance that looks more tropical than typical New England shrubs.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Bright yellow flowers appear in upright clusters at branch tips in early spring. Each small flower has 6 petals and gives off a light, sweet fragrance. The flower clusters are showy and stand out dramatically against the dark foliage.

idTips.label: Fruit
idTips.description: Blue-black berries about the size of small grapes, covered with a waxy bloom that makes them look dusty. They hang in grape-like clusters and ripen in late summer, often persisting into fall.

idTips.label: Bark
idTips.description: Stems are yellowish to light brown with a smooth texture when young, becoming slightly ridged with age. When scratched, the inner bark reveals a bright yellow color typical of the barberry family.

habitat: In New England, leatherleaf mahonia is extremely rare and typically found only as an escaped ornamental near old homesites or abandoned gardens. When it does establish, it prefers partially shaded areas with well-drained, slightly acidic soil. Look for it in woodland edges or naturalized areas where other non-native ornamentals have taken hold.

seasonality.spring: Bright yellow flower clusters appear in April to May, creating a stunning display against the evergreen foliage. This is the easiest time to spot the plant from a distance due to the showy blooms.
seasonality.summer: Flowers fade and small green berries begin developing. The thick, waxy leaves remain the primary identifying feature during the growing season.
seasonality.fall: Blue-black berries ripen and often persist on the plant. The evergreen leaves may take on slight bronze tints in colder weather but remain fundamentally green.
seasonality.winter: The plant remains fully evergreen, making it highly conspicuous in the winter landscape. The thick, spiny compound leaves and upright growth habit are easily identified even under snow.

funFact: The bright yellow color you see when you scratch the bark isn't just for show – it contains berberine, a compound that has been used in traditional medicine for thousands of years and is now being studied as a potential treatment for diabetes and heart disease.
confusionNotes: The thick, spiny compound leaves make this nearly impossible to confuse with any native New England plant. The closest lookalike might be Oregon grape (also a Berberis), but Oregon grape has smaller leaflets and a more spreading growth habit. Remember: if you see what looks like a holly bush with compound leaves, you've found something in the barberry family.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'mahonia' for decades, botanists now classify this plant as a true barberry (Berberis). You'll still see it sold in nurseries under the old name Mahonia bealei, which can be confusing. It's also worth noting that while this plant is rare in New England, it has become invasive in some southeastern states.
compareHints: Leatherleaf mahonia differs from Japanese barberry by being evergreen with large compound leaves, while Japanese barberry is deciduous with simple leaves. Unlike European barberry, which has thin leaves in clusters, leatherleaf mahonia has thick, waxy compound leaves. Oregon grape is similar but has smaller leaflets and a lower, more spreading growth habit rather than the tall, upright form of leatherleaf mahonia.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Unlike its relative European barberry which has larger, more elongated berries and serrated leaf edges, Japanese barberry has smaller, rounder berries and smooth-edged leaves.
Among New England barberries, European barberry stands out with its three-pronged spines and elongated berries, while Japanese barberry has single spines and round berries.
Oregon grape stands out from other barberries in New England by being evergreen - Japanese barberry and European barberry both lose their leaves in winter.
Unlike the invasive Japanese barberry which loses its leaves and has single spines, wintergreen barberry keeps its thick evergreen leaves and has three-pronged spines.
